reasoning_summary: Standard exchange-property proof, and the load-bearing chain holds. Removing e={x,y} from tree T1 splits V into VA (x) and VB (y) with e the unique T1 edge across the cut. The unique T2 path x=v0-...-vk=y must cross the cut, so f={v_{j-1},v_j} with v_{j-1} in VA, v_j in VB exists and is a T2 edge. T1' = (T1\{e}) union {f}: f joins the two components A,B so T1' is connected on V; since T1\{e} has no VA-VB path, adding f creates no cycle, and the edge count stays |V|-1. T2' = (T2\{f}) union {e}: f lies on the unique x-y path in T2, so deleting f separates x from y, e rejoins those two components, and no cycle arises because no x-y path survives in T2\{f} (uniqueness of tree paths). Both graphs are therefore connected, acyclic, spanning. I probed the degenerate case e in T1 intersect T2 (e.g. V={x,y}, T1=T2={{x,y}}, or V={x,y,z}, T1={xy,yz}, T2={xy,xz} with e=xy): there k=1 and f={x,y}=e, so the proof's parenthetical assertion 'f cannot belong to T1' (lines 0014-0016) is overstated -- its own justification only rules out f being a T1 edge other than e. But nothing downstream uses that assertion: with f=e the counts still give |E1'|=|E2'|=|V|-1 and the exchange returns T1 and T2 themselves, which are trees, and the connectivity/acyclicity arguments remain valid verbatim. Also checked that f in T1\{e} is impossible (e is the unique cut edge) and e in T2\{f} is impossible (e in T2 forces the x-y path to be e, hence f=e), so no edge-count collapse can occur. No counterexample to any claim the proof relies on.
